text: Forgive me, investigators: the chapter-house door will not open for me yet. The Saltmere Chapter is not founded; I will give you its code the moment it is. Hold your lanterns.
Welcome, investigators. Join The Saltmere Chapter with the code saltmere-r3.
Cass Moreau, Slink. Soot coat, borrowed gloves, lockpicks in the lining. I'm here for the debt, and for whatever is ringing under that mud. Mind your pockets, everyone. Not mine, yours.
Bram Okafor, ex-soldier. Whistle on a cord, army coat, and I'm told to stand in front of people. Signed up on my phone, waiting on the door, ma'am.

Dev Lindqvist, Occultist. Ink on my cuffs, salt on my coat, and a notebook that is never closed. My grandmother hummed a hymn no church owned, and I would very much like to know who taught her. Request to join sent, ma'am.
Welcome to the circle, Cass Moreau: your ledger is ash and your gloves are borrowed, so keep your hands where Bram can see them.
Welcome, Bram Okafor. The Chapter believes you, soldier; stand in front of them and they will stand behind you.
Welcome, Professor Pontius Aganus. The secrets of the deep have been waiting eighty years under Saltmere's mud; I trust your tome is waterproof.
Welcome, Dev Lindqvist. Bring your grandmother's hymn; I suspect Saltmere knows the tune.

Now, all four of you: the Circle Formation Papers will be lying open on your desks. Fill in all six parts together: vote a circle question and write your own answer, suggest and vote a name, write the chapter house, vote an ability and an insignia, and propose a relationship to each of the others (and answer theirs).
Tell me at the table when your papers are done. Once every part has a choice I will press the Lightkeeper's seal, and then the dispatch to Saltmere goes out.
A word before we begin: Professor Pontius Aganus has been called away and will not join us. Ada Quill takes the empty chair; I will bring her in shortly.

Ada Quill, Professor. Tweed gone shiny at the elbows, a pencil behind each ear, and a footnote the Dean wanted burned. I would like to know who taught Saltmere that hymn, and I intend to cite my sources. Request to join sent, ma'am.
Welcome to the circle, Professor Ada Quill. Saltmere's hymn has gone eighty years without a citation; I expect you to supply one.

A note from the Chapter's clerk: Pontius Aganus's name is still inked on our papers and the clerk cannot strike it out, so you will see him listed. Ignore his chair: do not wait for his vote and leave his relationship line empty.

Next: all five parts of the Circle Formation Papers on your desks (Ada, yours too now). Vote a question and write your answer, suggest and vote a name, one of you writes the chapter house, vote an ability and an insignia, and propose a relationship to each of the other three players. Say 'papers done' here; when all four of you have, I press the seal and the dispatch to Saltmere goes out.
Pardon the slip of my pen: six parts, not five (I. question, II. name, III. chapter house, IV. ability, V. insignia, VI. relationships).
Papers done on my end, ma'am: I backed the second question, voted Lantern Wall, Nobody Left Behind and Candlelight, and put my lines to Cass, Dev and Ada. Dev, the chapter house is yours.

Papers done on my end, ma'am: second question with my answer written, The Citation Society suggested (I voted Lantern Wall with Bram), Nobody Left Behind, Candlelight, and proposals to Cass, Bram and Dev; I accepted Bram's Mentor. Dev, the chapter house is yours. Cass, I am waiting on your line to me.

Papers done, ma'am: second question with my answer, voted The Lantern Wall (my own 'Mudlark Choir' suggestion, long and full of bells, lost the vote fair and square), Nobody Left Behind, Candlelight. Accepted Bram's Old Friend and Ada's Coworker; I proposed Confidant to Bram, Mentor to Dev, Rival to Ada. Dev, the chapter house is yours.

Papers done, ma'am: answered the second question (the hymn arriving in our own handwriting), voted Lantern Wall, Nobody Left Behind, Candlelight. I wrote the chapter house: a loft above the chandler's on Wick Lane, harmonium that hums at the turn of the tide. Accepted Cass's Mentor, Bram's Ward and Ada's Confidant, and proposed Rival to Cass, Champion to Bram, Muse to Ada. Pontius's line left empty.
The circle is sealed: you are The Lantern Wall, Candlelight on your coats and Nobody Left Behind in your bones. The dispatch is on your desks. Saltmere, the flats, dusk.

The tide has gone out further than any of the fishermen's wives can remember. The flats run grey and shining to the edge of the light, scored with gull tracks and the ribs of a drowned punt. Three lines of bootprints lead out from the slipway, deep and steady, and each one simply stops, mid-stride, as if the mud closed over a man and smoothed itself. Two hundred yards out a bell rope stands straight up out of the silt, stiff as a mast, frayed at the top. And as the last of the sun goes, the bells start: low, slow, under your feet, eighty years under the mud. A mudlark girl picking cockles at the edge of the flats has stopped working. She is humming. So, you notice, is the back of your own throat.

First actions, one each, on your desk's dice tray: Bram, you lead the way out toward the rope, testing the mud before the others step: roll Move (Nerve). Ada, you kneel at the end of the nearest line of prints and study the last one, and the rope beyond it, for anything a textbook would recognise: roll Focus (Intuition). Cass, the mudlark girl, Nell, is the only one here who watched a fisherman walk out: get her talking before the hymn takes her: roll Sway (Cunning). Dev, close your eyes and listen to the bells and the humming underneath them: what is this, and where is it strongest? roll Sense (Intuition). Spend drive if you like; tell me what you are doing as you roll.
I kneel at the end of the nearest line of prints, pencil behind my ear, and study the last print and the rope beyond it. I will spend one Intuition on it: Focus 2 plus one die, one of them gilded.
I wade out first, testing each step with the butt of my rifle before I put my weight down. Spending a point of Nerve on it. Stay behind me, and step where I step.
Mixed success, ma'am: I kept the 4. The mud holds, but slow and sucking; I find a firm line out toward the rope and wave the others on, boots sinking to the shin.
I crouch by Nell, the mudlark girl, and offer her a pinch of rock salt and a sixpence. 'You saw him go, love. Which way did he walk, and was he humming too?' I'll spend a point of Cunning on it.
I close my eyes and let the salt on my coat settle. The bells first, then under them the humming, and I listen for the tune my grandmother hummed. I spend two Intuition and roll Sense.

A clean six, ma'am (4 dice, two Intuition spent). The bells are not one bell but many, and the humming is strongest not at the rope but beneath the slipway behind us, as if the singers are under the whole shore. And it is my grandmother's tune, a verse early.

Nell, a 4: she talks, but not all of it. 'He weren't walking, miss. He were *following*. And he were humming the same as you are now.' She backs a step toward the slipway, still humming. I keep a hand on my lockpicks and a sixpence out.

Bram, a 4: you find the firm line, but the mud takes its price. Each step sucks at your boots to the shin, and when you reach the rope and pull your rifle butt free it comes up wrapped in a scrap of white linen: a surplice, choir-white, eighty years in the silt and still clean. The rope is warm to the touch.

Ada, a 2: the last print is wrong in a way no textbook has a plate for. The toes point back toward the shore, as if the man turned in his own footprint and was walked out backwards. You lean closer to measure it, and the bells come up through your knees and into your teeth. For a moment you cannot remember the word for 'rope'. Take a Brain mark, Professor (it is on your sheet). And check your desk: you heard something the others did not.

Cass, a 4: Nell talks, and then the mud moves. The silt heaves under her bare feet and she drops to the knee, still humming. Bram's line and your grip on her wrist are enough: she comes free with a sound like a cork. 'Choirmaster's rooms,' she gasps, 'Wick Lane, over the chandler's. Mr Abel's been humming in there since Tuesday and he's been dead since my nan was a girl.' Then she runs.

Dev, a 6, and it changes everything: the bells are under the whole shore, strongest beneath the slipway, and the verse your grandmother hummed is the next one, the one the choir has not reached yet. The bell rope jerks down a full foot into the mud as you open your eyes. Something below knows you are listening. The hourglass turns: tension 1 of 4.

Scene 2. Wick Lane, full dark. The chandler's shop below your own loft, and between the two a door you have walked past every day and never seen open: the old choirmaster's lodging, Mr Abel's. The new dispatch is on your desks. Inside it is cold and smells of tallow and river. A music stand by the window holds a hymn sheet, 'For the Low Water', and the hand that wrote it changes halfway down the page: neat copperplate above, then something cramped and wet-looking below. In the corner, a tall music cabinet, locked, its keyhole crusted with salt. And the humming is louder here than it was on the flats. Through the ceiling, faintly, your own harmonium answers it.

One action each: Ada, the hymn sheet is yours: read where the hand changes and what the lower hand is really writing: roll Read (Cunning). Cass, the music cabinet: pick that salt-crusted lock without snapping a pick: roll Control (Nerve). Bram, stand at the window and watch the lane and the room both; something keeps moving at the edge of your eye: roll Survey (Intuition). Dev, there is a choirmaster's daybook on the desk in old notation and older symbols: make sense of it: roll Focus (Intuition). Spend drive if you like; tell me what you do as you roll. Bram, if your desk ever offers you 'Behind Me' for someone's mark, that choice is yours to take or leave.
